title: Regular expressions
subtitle: Find, validate and extract text patterns
goal: Write regular expressions to search, validate, extract and clean text, and know when a simpler tool is the better choice.
outcomes: Use re.search, match, fullmatch, findall, finditer, sub and split
Build patterns from character classes, quantifiers and anchors
Pull structured data out of text with groups and named groups
Validate Indian mobile numbers, PIN codes and emails
Recognise when string methods or a parser beat a regex

slides.title: Mission 33: Pattern power
slides.body:
A **regular expression** (regex) is a tiny language for describing text patterns: *"ten digits starting with 6 to 9"*.

It powers form validation, log analysis, search-and-replace in every code editor, and data cleaning.

left.title: By hand
left.code:
ok = (len(p) == 10 and p.isdigit()
      and p[0] in "6789")

visual.verdict: One readable pattern replaces a pile of checks, and it scales to harder formats.

slides.say: A regular expression, or regex, is a tiny language for describing patterns in text, like ten digits that start with six, seven, eight or nine. Regex powers form validation, log analysis, and search and replace in every code editor. Today you will read and write patterns, and learn when not to use them.

slides.title: Building blocks
slides.body:
Write patterns as **raw strings** `r"..."` so backslashes reach the regex untouched.

`re.search(pattern, text)` finds the first match anywhere and returns a **Match** object, or `None`.

head: Token
Matches
Example
rows: one char NOT in the set

slides.say: Always write patterns as raw strings, with a small r before the quotes, so Python leaves the backslashes alone. Then learn a handful of building blocks. Backslash d means any digit. Backslash w means a letter, digit or underscore. Square brackets mean one character from a set, like six to nine. And a dot means any character at all.

slides.title: Your first search
slides.code:
import re

msg = "Your OTP is 482913. Do not share it."
m = re.search(r"\d{6}", msg)
print(m)
print(m.group(), m.start(), m.end())

print(re.search(r"\d{6}", "No code here"))
explain: \d{6}: exactly six digits in a row.
A Match object shows where it matched and what.
group() is the matched text; start/end are positions.
No match gives None: check before calling .group().
slides.say: Here we pull a six digit OTP out of an SMS, the same thing your phone does when it offers to autofill a code. Search returns a match object. Group gives the matched text, and start and end give its position. When nothing matches you get None, so always check before using the result.

slides.title: Quantifiers and anchors
slides.say: Quantifiers say how many times the previous piece repeats. Plus means one or more, star means zero or more, a question mark means optional, and curly brackets give an exact count or a range. Anchors match positions rather than characters: the caret is the start, the dollar sign is the end, and backslash b is the edge of a word.

slides.title: findall: extract every match
slides.code:
import re

sms = "Paid Rs 450 to Ravi, Rs 1200 to Meera and Rs 85 to Metro"
amounts = re.findall(r"Rs (\d+)", sms)
print(amounts)
print(sum(int(a) for a in amounts))

tags = re.findall(r"#\w+", "Loving #Python and #100DaysOfCode!")
print(tags)
explain: Brackets make a group: findall returns only the group's text.
Matches are strings: convert before adding.
#\w+: a hash sign, then one or more word characters.
slides.say: Findall returns every match as a list of strings. Notice the brackets in the first pattern: they form a group, and when a pattern has one group, findall returns just that part, the number without the R s. Matches are always strings, so convert them before doing maths. The second pattern finds hashtags: a hash sign followed by one or more word characters.

slides.title: Predict: greedy matching
slides.code: import re html = "Hi and Bye" print(re.findall(r"(.*)", html))
slides.why: `.*` is greedy: it grabs as much as possible, all the way to the last . Add `?` to make it lazy: `.*?` stops at the first and gives ['Hi', 'Bye']. (For real HTML, use a parser: Day 52.)
slides.say: A classic surprise. We want the text inside each bold tag. Dot star means any characters, as many as possible. Predict what findall returns.

slides.title: match, search or fullmatch?
slides.body: For **validation**, use `fullmatch`. A `search` happily finds a valid number inside `"call 98765432101 now"`.
slides.say: Three ways to apply a pattern. Match only checks at the very start of the text. Search looks anywhere. Full match demands that the whole text fits the pattern. For validating user input, always use full match, otherwise search will happily find a valid looking number hidden inside garbage.

slides.title: Validate Indian mobile numbers
slides.code:
import re

MOBILE = re.compile(r"(?:\+91[\s-]?)?[6-9]\d{9}")

numbers = ["9876543210", "+91 9876543210", "+91-7012345678",
           "5876543210", "98765432101"]
for phone in numbers:
    ok = MOBILE.fullmatch(phone) is not None
    print(f"{phone:<15} {ok}")
explain: Compile once, reuse often. (?:...) groups without capturing; \+ is a literal plus; [\s-]? allows one space or dash.
fullmatch: the whole string must be a mobile number.
:<15 pads the text to line up the results.
slides.say: Indian mobile numbers have ten digits and start with six, seven, eight or nine, optionally with plus nine one in front. Re dot compile builds the pattern once so you can reuse it. The part in brackets starting with a question mark and colon groups the prefix without capturing it, and the question mark after it makes the whole prefix optional.

slides.title: Fix the bug: PIN codes
slides.task: Indian PIN codes are exactly **6 digits** and never start with 0. `is_valid_pin` accepts `"4110012"` and `"PIN 411001"`. Fix it.
slides.starter:
import re

def is_valid_pin(pin):
    # 6 digits, the first one 1-9
    return re.search(r"[1-9]\d{5}", pin) is not None

print(is_valid_pin("411001"), is_valid_pin("4110012"))
slides.solution:
import re

def is_valid_pin(pin):
    # 6 digits, the first one 1-9
    return re.fullmatch(r"[1-9]\d{5}", pin) is not None

print(is_valid_pin("411001"), is_valid_pin("4110012"))
slides.tests:
assert is_valid_pin("411001") is True, "411001 (Pune) is a valid PIN code and should return True."
assert is_valid_pin("110001") is True, "110001 (New Delhi) is valid too."
assert is_valid_pin("4110012") is False, "4110012 has 7 digits. search finds 6 valid digits inside it: use fullmatch so the whole text must match."
assert is_valid_pin("PIN 411001") is False, "Extra text around the digits should make it invalid."
assert is_valid_pin("041100") is False, "A PIN code never starts with 0."
assert is_valid_pin("") is False, "An empty string is not a PIN code."
hints: search looks for the pattern anywhere inside the text.
Switch to re.fullmatch so the whole string has to be the PIN code.
slides.say: Bug hunt. A delivery app is accepting PIN codes with seven digits, and even ones with extra text. The pattern itself is fine. The problem is which function applies it. Fix it so only a complete, six digit PIN passes.

slides.title: Groups and named groups
slides.body:
Parentheses **capture** parts of a match. Name them with `(?P<name>...)` and read them by name:

- `m.group("year")`
- `m.groupdict()` gives a dict of every named group
slides.say: Brackets do more than group: they capture. Each captured part can be read separately from the match. Even better, give a group a name with question mark, capital P, and the name in angle brackets. Then you read it by name, or ask for group dict to get a dictionary of every named part. It is the cleanest way to turn a line of text into data.

slides.title: Parse a log with named groups
slides.code:
import re

log = '''2026-10-18 09:12:01 ERROR payment failed code=502
2026-10-18 09:12:05 INFO retry scheduled
2026-10-18 09:13:44 ERROR payment failed code=504'''

LINE = re.compile(r"(?P<time>\d\d:\d\d:\d\d) (?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<msg>.*)")
for m in LINE.finditer(log):
    if m.group("level") == "ERROR":
        print(m.group("time"), "->", m.group("msg"))

print(LINE.search(log).groupdict())
explain: Three named groups: time, level and msg.
finditer yields Match objects one by one.
Read groups by name: clear and robust.
groupdict(): every named group in a dict.
slides.say: A real log, three lines. Our pattern names three parts: the time, the level and the message. Finditer walks through every match one at a time, lazily, which is ideal for big log files. Notice dot star stops at the end of each line, because a dot never matches a newline.

slides.title: sub and split: clean and mask
slides.code:
import re

card = "Card 4111 1111 1111 1234 charged"
print(re.sub(r"\d{4} \d{4} \d{4} (\d{4})", r"XXXX XXXX XXXX \1", card))

messy = "  too    many   spaces  "
print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", messy).strip())

print(re.split(r"[,;|]\s*", "chai, coffee;tea|lassi"))
slides.expect:
Card XXXX XXXX XXXX 1234 charged
too many spaces
['chai', 'coffee', 'tea', 'lassi']
explain: \1 in the replacement inserts group 1: the last four digits.
\s+ matches any run of whitespace.
Split on comma, semicolon or pipe, plus any spaces after it.
slides.say: Sub means substitute. The first example masks a card number before it goes into a log, keeping only the last four digits. Backslash one in the replacement puts back whatever group one captured. The second squeezes runs of spaces into one. And split breaks text on any of several separators at once, which plain string split cannot do.

slides.title: Predict: flags
slides.code:
import re

text = "Python python PYTHON"
print(len(re.findall(r"python", text)), len(re.findall(r"python", text, re.I)))
slides.why: Regex is case-sensitive by default, so only the lowercase 'python' matches. The flag re.I (re.IGNORECASE) makes the pattern ignore case, so all three match.
slides.say: Flags change how a pattern behaves. Re dot I is short for ignore case. How many matches do we get without the flag, and with it?

slides.title: Readable patterns with re.VERBOSE
slides.body: `re.VERBOSE` ignores spaces and allows comments inside the pattern. Other useful flags: `re.IGNORECASE`, `re.MULTILINE` (`^` and `$` match at every line).
slides.code:
import re

EMAIL = re.compile(r"""
    [\w.+-]+        # name: letters, digits, dot, plus, dash
    @
    [\w-]+          # domain
    (\.[\w-]+)+     # one or more parts like .co.in
""", re.VERBOSE)

for e in ["riya.s@gmail.com", "dev+test@brodoit.co.in", "no-at-sign.com", "a@b"]:
    print(f"{e:<24} {bool(EMAIL.fullmatch(e))}")
slides.expect:
riya.s@gmail.com         True
dev+test@brodoit.co.in   True
no-at-sign.com           False
a@b                      False
explain: A triple-quoted raw string spread over several lines.
Comments explain each piece.
Group repeated with +: .co, then .in.
re.VERBOSE: whitespace in the pattern is ignored.
bool() turns a Match or None into True or False.
slides.say: Long patterns become unreadable fast. The verbose flag lets you spread a pattern over several lines with comments, and it ignores the spaces. One honest warning: no regex can prove an email address really exists. Use a simple pattern to catch typos, then send a confirmation link. That is what every serious app does.

slides.title: When NOT to use regex
slides.body:
*"Some people, when confronted with a problem, think 'I know, I'll use regular expressions.' Now they have two problems."*

- simple checks: `startswith`, `endswith`, `in`, `isdigit`
- JSON, CSV, HTML: use a **parser**
- dates: `strptime`; numbers: `int()` in a `try`

visual.verdict: Same result, and anyone on the team can read the right-hand version instantly.

slides.say: There is a famous joke among programmers: some people, faced with a problem, think I know, I will use regular expressions. Now they have two problems. Regex is powerful but hard to read. If a string method does the job, use it. For JSON, CSV and HTML, use a real parser. For dates use strptime, and for numbers use int inside a try.

slides.title: Right tool for the job
slides.q: You need to check that an uploaded file name ends in .csv. What's the best choice?
slides.why: A string method is clearer, faster and harder to get wrong. Note the third option even accepts 'mycsv' with no dot. Save regex for real patterns.
slides.say: Quick check. You only need to know whether a file name ends in dot c s v. Which option would a senior developer choose?

slides.title: Clean up mobile numbers
slides.task:
Users type numbers like `"+91 98765 43210"` or `"098765-43210"`. Write `normalize_mobile(text)` that returns the plain **10-digit** number, or `None` if it isn't a valid Indian mobile.

- remove spaces and dashes
- allow an optional `+91`, `91` or `0` prefix
- the 10 digits must start with 6–9
slides.starter:
import re

def normalize_mobile(text):
    # 1. remove spaces and dashes with re.sub
    # 2. fullmatch an optional prefix and capture the 10 digits
    return None

print(normalize_mobile("+91 98765 43210"))
slides.solution:
import re

def normalize_mobile(text):
    digits = re.sub(r"[\s-]", "", text)
    m = re.fullmatch(r"(?:\+91|91|0)?([6-9]\d{9})", digits)
    return m.group(1) if m else None

print(normalize_mobile("+91 98765 43210"))
slides.tests:
cases = {"+91 98765 43210": "9876543210", "098765-43210": "9876543210",
         "9876543210": "9876543210", "919812345678": "9812345678"}
for raw, want in cases.items():
    got = normalize_mobile(raw)
    assert got == want, f"normalize_mobile({raw!r}) should return {want!r}, got {got!r}."
assert normalize_mobile("12345 67890") is None, "Mobile numbers start with 6, 7, 8 or 9: '12345 67890' should give None."
assert normalize_mobile("+91 9876543210 1") is None, "That's 11 digits after +91: return None. Use fullmatch, not search."
assert normalize_mobile("") is None, "An empty string should give None."
hints: Remove separators first: digits = re.sub(r"[\s-]", "", text)
Then m = re.fullmatch(r"(?:\+91|91|0)?([6-9]\d{9})", digits) and return m.group(1) when it matched.
slides.say: Sign-up forms receive phone numbers in every format imaginable. Write normalize mobile: strip spaces and dashes, allow an optional plus nine one, nine one or zero in front, and return the clean ten digits. Anything else returns None.

slides.title: Turn payment SMS into data
slides.task:
Write `parse_payment(sms)` that reads messages like:

`Sent Rs 1,250.00 to Ravi Kumar on 18-10-2026. UPI Ref 612345678901`

Return a dict with `amount` (float), `to`, `date` and `ref` (strings). Return `None` if the SMS doesn't match. Use **named groups**.
slides.starter:
import re

# TODO: finish the pattern with named groups amount, to, date and ref
PAYMENT = re.compile(r"Sent Rs (?P<amount>[\d,.]+) to ")

def parse_payment(sms):
    return None

print(parse_payment("Sent Rs 1,250.00 to Ravi Kumar on 18-10-2026. UPI Ref 612345678901"))
slides.solution:
import re

PAYMENT = re.compile(
    r"Sent Rs (?P<amount>[\d,]+\.\d{2}) to (?P<to>.+?) on "
    r"(?P<date>\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{4})\. UPI Ref (?P<ref>\d{12})"
)

def parse_payment(sms):
    m = PAYMENT.search(sms)
    if m is None:
        return None
    data = m.groupdict()
    data["amount"] = float(data["amount"].replace(",", ""))
    return data

print(parse_payment("Sent Rs 1,250.00 to Ravi Kumar on 18-10-2026. UPI Ref 612345678901"))
slides.tests:
r1 = parse_payment("Sent Rs 1,250.00 to Ravi Kumar on 18-10-2026. UPI Ref 612345678901")
want1 = {"amount": 1250.0, "to": "Ravi Kumar", "date": "18-10-2026", "ref": "612345678901"}
assert r1 == want1, f"Expected {want1}, got {r1}. Remove the commas before float()."
r2 = parse_payment("Alert: Sent Rs 12,00,000.00 to Meera Iyer on 01-11-2026. UPI Ref 700000000123")
assert r2 is not None and r2["amount"] == 1200000.0, f"Lakh-style commas: 12,00,000.00 is 1200000.0. Got {r2}."
assert r2["to"] == "Meera Iyer" and r2["ref"] == "700000000123", f"Names can have spaces; ref is the 12 digits. Got {r2}."
assert parse_payment("Your OTP is 482913") is None, "An SMS that isn't a payment should return None."
hints: Finish the pattern: ... to (?P<to>.+?) on (?P<date>\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{4})\. UPI Ref (?P<ref>\d{12})
m.groupdict() gives you the dict; then convert amount with float(text.replace(",", "")).
Use search, not fullmatch, so extra words like 'Alert:' before the message are fine.
slides.say: Expense apps read your payment messages and turn them into data. Write parse payment with named groups for the amount, the person, the date and the reference number. Convert the amount to a float, and watch out for Indian style commas in lakhs.

slides.title: Mission 33 complete
points: Write patterns as raw strings; search finds, findall and finditer extract, sub replaces, split splits
Classes like \d \w \s [6-9], quantifiers + * ? {n}, and anchors ^ $ \b describe text
Validate with fullmatch, never plain search
Named groups and groupdict turn text into structured data
Prefer string methods and real parsers when they are clearer
slides.say: Mission thirty three complete. You can search, extract, validate and clean text with regular expressions, and you know when a string method or a parser is the wiser choice. Tomorrow we make our code say exactly what it means, with type hints, data classes and enums. See you on day thirty four.
